summary: 是 shì links a subject to a noun: 我是学生 ‘I am a student’. It never changes (我是, 你是, 他们是 — present or past) and is negated with 不: 不是 bú shì. Two other jobs of ‘to be’ are done with other means: before an adjective Chinese uses no verb at all (我很好 ‘I am fine’ — never *我是好), and ‘to be somewhere’ is 在 zài: 老师在这里 ‘the teacher is here’.

blocks.caption: ‘To be’ in Chinese

blocks.title: No 是 before adjectives
blocks.text: 我很好, 她很高 — adjectives act like verbs. *我是好 is a typical beginner’s mistake (adjectives come in S16).

items.title: 是 — what something is
points: 我是老师。 I am a teacher.
这是门。 This is a door.

items.title: 在 — where something is
points: 老师在这里。 The teacher is here.
钥匙不在这里。 The keys are not here.

blocks.title: No articles after 是
blocks.text: ‘I am a student’ is 我是学生 — no word for ‘a’ is needed.

askYourself: Is the thing after ‘to be’ a noun (what someone or something is)? → 是.
Is it an adjective (how something is)? → no 是: 我很好.
Is it a place (where something is)? → 在: 他在这里.
Is the sentence negative? → 不是 / 不在 (bú shì, bú zài).
Does the verb change for person or time? → never.
steps: Choose 是 (noun), nothing (adjective) or 在 (place).
Negate with 不 directly before it.

traps: *我是好 / *我是很好 → 我很好.
*他没是老师 → 他不是老师 (是 is negated with 不 only).
*我是一个老师 is possible but usually just 我是老师 — no ‘a’ needed.

quiz.why: A noun after ‘to be’ needs 是.
是 is negated with 不, placed right before it.
不 becomes bú before the 4th tone.

notes.text: Greek είμαι conjugates (είμαι, είσαι, είναι) and serves nouns, adjectives and places alike (είμαι φοιτητής, είμαι καλά, είμαι στο σπίτι). Chinese splits these: 是 before a noun, no verb before an adjective (我很好), 在 for a place (我在家).

Russian drops ‘to be’ in the present (Я студент), but Chinese needs 是 between two nouns: 我是学生. Before an adjective Chinese drops it as Russian does (Она высокая ~ 她很高). And ‘there is’ (есть) is 有, not 是.

Spanish already splits ‘to be’: ser for what something is (soy estudiante ~ 我是学生), estar for where it is (estoy en casa ~ 我在家). Chinese adds a third way: before an adjective there is no verb at all (estoy cansado ~ 我很累).
English uses ‘be’ for nouns (I am a student), adjectives (I am tired) and places (I am at home). Chinese uses three patterns: 我是学生, 我很累 (no verb), 我在家.
French être covers c’est un livre, je suis fatigué and je suis à la maison; Chinese splits them into 这是书, 我很累 (no verb) and 我在家.

German sein conjugates (bin, bist, ist) and serves nouns, adjectives and places; Chinese 是 is only for nouns, adjectives take no verb (ich bin müde ~ 我很累), and being somewhere is 在 (ich bin zu Hause ~ 我在家).

Hindi ends such sentences with है / हूँ / हैं, which change with person (मैं छात्र हूँ ‘I am a student’), and uses them with adjectives too. Chinese 是 stands between the nouns, never changes, and is left out before adjectives.
Persian -am / -i / ast change with person (man dāneshjuam ‘I am a student’) and also stand after adjectives (khasteam ‘I’m tired’). Chinese 是 never changes and is left out before adjectives: 我很累.

Marathi आहे comes at the end and serves nouns, adjectives and places (मी विद्यार्थी आहे, मी घरी आहे). Chinese 是 stands between the nouns, never changes, and has two partners: no verb before adjectives, 在 for places.

Arabic has no ‘is’ in the present (anā ṭālib ‘I am a student’), and kāna changes with person and tense. Chinese needs 是 between two nouns, in every tense, and it never changes; before adjectives Chinese, like Arabic, has no verb.

Hebrew leaves out ‘to be’ in the present (ani student, ha-bayit gadol) and uses haya in the past and future. Chinese links two nouns with 是 in every tense; with adjectives it agrees with Hebrew — no verb (房子很大).

Turkish makes ‘to be’ an ending on the noun (öğrenciyim ‘I am a student’) and leaves it out in the 3rd person (o öğrenci). Chinese uses the separate word 是 in every person (他是学生), and ‘I am at home’ (evdeyim) is the verb 在: 我在家.
Japanese i-adjectives are predicates by themselves (高い ‘is tall’), just as Chinese 他很高 needs no 是. だ / です after a noun matches 是; いる / ある for being somewhere match 在.
Korean descriptive verbs (크다 ‘be big’) need no copula, like Chinese adjectives; 이다 (학생이에요) matches 是. Korean 있다 is both ‘be at’ and ‘have’ — Chinese splits these into 在 and 有.
Finnish olla serves everything and conjugates (olen opiskelija, olen väsynyt, olen kotona). Chinese splits it: 是 + noun, a bare adjective with 很, 在 + place.

Hungarian leaves out ‘is’ in the 3rd person before nouns and adjectives (Ő tanár, A ház nagy) but uses van for a place (otthon van). Chinese leaves it out before adjectives in every person (我很好), keeps 是 before nouns, and 在 does the work of van.

Swahili ni is an unchanging copula like 是 (mimi ni mwalimu ‘I am a teacher’), but it also stands before adjectives (yeye ni mrefu ‘he is tall’), where Chinese has no verb (他很高). Being somewhere is -ko (yuko nyumbani ‘he is at home’) — 在 in Chinese.

Luganda -li ‘be’ takes the person prefix (ndi ‘I am’, oli ‘you are’, ali ‘he / she is’) and serves qualities and places. Chinese has one unchanging 是 for nouns, no verb before adjectives, and 在 for places.
Vietnamese works the same way: là before a noun (tôi là sinh viên ~ 我是学生), no verb before an adjective (tôi mệt ~ 我很累), and ở for a place (tôi ở nhà ~ 我在家).
Inuktitut makes ‘be a teacher’ one verb word: a ‘be’ suffix on the noun plus the person ending. Chinese keeps three separate, unchanging words: 我 + 是 + 老师.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has no ‘is’ in the present: ana ṭālib ‘I (am) a student’ — Chinese needs 是 between two nouns.
Hebrew too: ani talmid ‘I (am) a pupil’; and like Chinese, nothing stands before an adjective.
German sein conjugates (bin, bist, ist, sind) and is also used before adjectives (ich bin müde) — Chinese 我很累 has no verb.
